text:
In the Court of Appeal of Alberta

Citation: R. v. Keegstra, 1996 ABCA 308

Date:
19960926

Docket:
13544

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

Appellant

- and -

James Keegstra

Respondent

The Court:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Kerans

The Honourable Mr. Justice Agrios

The Honourable Mr. Justice Mason

Memorandum of Judgment

COUNSEL:

J. S. Koval, Q.C., for the Appellant

Douglas Christie, for the Respondent

MEMORANDUM OF
JUDGMENT

THE COURT:

[
1
]

This is an appeal by the Crown from the sentence
imposed upon the accused after his conviction, by a jury, on this charge:

The accused, James Keegstra, between the
1st day of September, A.D. 1978 and the 31st day of December, A.D. 1982,
inclusive at or near the Town of Eckville in the Province of Alberta, did unlawfully
promote hatred against an identifiable group, to wit: the Jewish people, by
communicating statements while teaching to students at Eckville High School
contrary to the provisions of the
Criminal Code
.

[
2
]

The accused, for all the years within the scope
of the charge, taught social studies in an Alberta high school. It was proven against him that he had repeatedly
sought to inflame his students against the Jewish people. Several of the
students, now adults, testified at trial. The Court also had the benefit of the
classroom notes of several students over several years. This left beyond doubt
that the accused regularly vilified the Jewish people in history. His remarks
were filled with references to cabals, secret societies, and conspiracies, all
of which were offered as historical fact and not as matter of religious belief.
He sought to implicate the Jewish people for almost every event in recent
history, including the Cromwellian, French, American, and Russian Revolutions,
the rise of Bismarck, the Great
Depression, and both world wars. His stories amount to a half-baked rehash of
every calumny or slander against the Jewish people over the course of western
history, of which we must sadly acknowledge there have been many. Just by way
of example, one student recalled at trial that the accused offered this
true/false exam question:

A:     Number 3, the Jews generally are - were good citizens.

Q:     What answer did you give?

A:     I gave false.

Q:     And what was Mr. Keegstra’s response to that?

A:     I had it correct. [A.B. 273]

[
3
]

She recalled him saying that”… Cromwell let the
Jews into England. And that was
the beginning of the end for England”. [A.B. 236]. And,”… The Jews have been out to kill us for a long
time…”. [A.B. 248] And, “The Jews were the cause of Germany’s troubles…” (A.B. 252) About the Holocaust, she recalled:

Mr. Keegstra just told us stuff that --
like the Holocaust didn’t really happen, and that the photography was all trick
photography … [A.B.525].

[
4
]

The trial judge ordered the accused to pay a
fine of $3,000. He correctly said that what he called “repudiation” and
deterrence were the paramount sentencing factors in a case like this. By “repudiation”,
he explained, he meant that the severity of the sentence should reflect the
public’s view of the seriousness of the crime. He also correctly observed that
the hate law has in mind to protect the impressionable from exposure to the
promotion of hatred. He said that the students had apparently become productive
members of society, which suggests that he doubted if any had been much touched
by the poison taught them. He said that in this case unlike others the effort
to promote hatred was confined to “a small group”. He then concluded,

Any punishment I now impose is slight, if
of any effect, compared with the loss of your teaching certificate, your loss
of reputation, and the scorn that you have suffered as you have been ground
through 10 years in the court system, and will suffer in the future.

[
5
]

Apparently for this reason, he decided that the
sentence he imposed was adequate.

[
6
]

The Crown on appeal contended that this
disposition is manifestly inadequate for this serious crime. It was said that
any lack of success by the accused in his attempts to promote hatred should not
count in his favour, and that the crime is very serious when committed by a
teacher with respect to his students, in breach of the great trust imposed upon
the teacher not to mislead impressionable and earnest young people.

[
7
]

Mr. Koval for the Crown also queried the opening
remarks in the sentencing reasons of the trial judge, when he said to the
accused “you fought the good fight”. It was said that this suggested that
somehow his rejected defence had merit and was not deserving of condemnation.
And Mr Koval challenged the comment that the accused has been “ground through …
the court system”, as though somehow the accused is a victim. Similarly, he
complained that the reference to “scorn” and “loss of reputation” hint that the
criminal is somehow the victim of the natural public reaction to his crime. The
Crown asks for a “condign” imprisonment.

[
8
]

Mr. Christie for the accused said that the
reference to “fighting the good fight” was merely a recognition by the judge
that the accused is sincere and honest, if misguided. He complained that Canada’s hate law allows the conviction of
sincere and honest persons who “might be telling the truth”. He said that the
Crown had not proven that what was said to the students was not true, and
lamented the intolerance he saw implicit in this law. He said that the accused
was a good teacher, who offered interesting challenges to his students. In his
factum, he argued that the teaching had no effect on the attitude of the
students towards the Jewish people, but also argued that “some students
testified that what he had taught on the conspiracy theory of history fit with
what they had experienced in life” and that “he had the facts to back up what
he said”. He argued that the law does not require for conviction that the
accused succeed in any attempt to promote hatred, and in this case no harm was
proven. But he conceded that the witness Lightbown “testified that she came out
of the course with an awareness of Jews which was not positive.”

[
9
]

Mr. Christie said that, but for this passionate
belief about a Jewish conspiracy, the accused, who is now 62, had led a
blameless life and always worked and supported his family and his community.

[
10
]

He also summarized what happened to the accused
after his classroom activities became well known, which occurred several years
before he was charged. He ceased to be Mayor of Eckville, and was dismissed as
a teacher. He also lost his teaching licence, and has for the past ten years
worked in a garage. He said that the accused has been impoverished, and
routinely vilified in the media. Mr. Christie added that somebody had burned
the accused’s house.

[
11
]

We agree with the Crown that, despite the
previous good record of the accused, the crime here deserves a sentence of
imprisonment in order to express society’s unconditional rejection of
hatemongering, to emphasize the harm to society done by those who preach racial
hatred, and to deter those of a like mind. We agree also that the fact that the
accused promoted hatred to his students in his high school classes over several
years was an aggravating factor, not a mitigating factor. Moreover, when he
committed these crimes, he was not “fighting the good fight”; he was attempting
to twist the minds of young people. And the people of Canada rightly scorn his crime, and him for never evincing the slightest
remorse or regret.

[
12
]

In fairness to the sentencing judge, we think
that he meant by his reference to a “good fight” merely to describe the jury
verdict to the accused in terms he might accept. He had testified at length in
an attempt to convince the jury of the reasonableness of his activity. But the
remark was unfortunate when viewed in the larger context.

[
13
]

We emphasize that, at trial, the accused
admitted that he had said most of what was claimed by the students or seen in
their notes, but sought to establish that everything he said was reasonable. He
failed utterly to move the jury, as he failed equally to move them with his
repeated pleas that he was a good teacher, merely giving them a more balanced
view of history than that offered by “mainstream” historians. The verdict must
be taken as an affirmation that the jury had no doubt that the accused did what
he did and said what he said in order to inflame his students and lead them to
hate the Jewish people. This is worthy of note because, again before us, he
persists in his pathetic and rejected claim that he is merely an honest student
of history.

[
14
]

We also should emphasize that the accused Keegstra
is not a harmless eccentric. He would have us all believe what he claims, and
would have us all believe all manner of hateful things about the Jewish people.
He also knew that what he was doing was forbidden by his employers. But he
arrogantly believes that he knows better than everyone, his employers, the
Courts, Parliament, all his fellow Canadians. There is only one word to describe
such behaviour. It is so perverse that it is evil.

[
15
]

The saddest part of this story is that some of
his students admit that he had an impact. While most claim they ignored him as
most students claim they ignore teachers, some acknowledged that they cannot
rid themselves of a sense of doubt about the Jewish people that he planted in
their minds.

[
16
]

We should do well to remember to distinguish the
accused Keegstra “case” from the accused Keegstra. The case stirred a debate in
Canada about the limits of free
speech, about what “truths” are beyond pubic debate, and about the marketplace
of ideas. But one should not associate the accused with the more libertarian
view expressed during that debate. In his work as a teacher, he showed a
reckless disregard for the truth. He heaped abuse on the Jewish people in
complete disregard, as came out clearly at trial, of any and all conflicting
opinion. And he would show no tolerance of anybody who disagreed with him. He
did not give the Jewish people the benefit of a careful inquiry into the
fairness of the claims he made against them. Nor did he make any effort to
offer what he had to say in Mr. Christie’s vaunted marketplace of ideas, where
he would, of course, suffer public scrutiny, and criticism. He slyly used
instead his dominant position in the classroom with children. And yet he was so
certain of his cause that he was prepared not just to debate the point, but to
actively promote hatred of his perceived enemies. In the cases about the
constitutional validity of this law, the dispute between this Court and the
Supreme Court of Canada was about the scope of possible prosecution under Canada’s hate law. This Court said the hate
law was too broad because its net would catch the harmless eccentric. But the
accused Keegstra is not, as we have said, a harmless eccentric.

[
17
]

We reject again Mr. Christie’s persistent
attacks on the law that the accused offended, attacks repeated again during
sentence submissions. Promotion of hatred of discreet groups is a crime in Canada because widespread hatred of
discreet groups is the antithesis of democracy. Democracy is all about the
right of every person in our society to equal respect and dignity. A democracy
is not the happiest society for a zealot, a person who thinks he knows all
truth and is so certain of his knowledge that he would suppress all opposition
as wrong and therefore evil. A democracy is a happier place for a tolerant
person, who may have equally strong beliefs about what is right and what is
true but who is willing to treat with respect those of a different mind, and
use only rational persuasion to correct their thinking. Mr Christie before us
commented upon the paradox of a law that, in the name of free speech, forbids
some speech. But the greater paradox is offered by the argument that the
principle of free speech justifies freedom for those who would end free speech.
In any event, there is no great paradox about a hate law as a bulwark of a free
society so long as we keep in mind that group hatred is the enemy of freedom.
When people in society hate a group, they tend to tolerate scorn and disrespect
toward the members of the group, who thereby become social outcasts and the
victims of all manner of indignities, including the loss of a voice in public
debate. In short, although they never go to prison, the victims of hatred lose
their freedom. The hate law seeks to preserve their freedom The Canadian hate
law condemns hatred of groups defined by race, gender, religion, or ethnic
origin simply because in the recent history of western society these are the
kinds of hatred that have led to persons ceasing to have civil rights in any
meaningful sense. It is not, sadly, a complete list. But it is a list of
occasions for irrational hatred that our society has rejected as essential if democracy
shall be preserved. There have been few charges laid in Canada under this law,
but we do not have to look too far beyond our frontiers to be reminded how easy
it is in this age to stir race and religious hatred to the murderous level that
destroys civil society. In sum, in Canada the right to free speech is not an absolute right.

[
18
]

We should also emphasize the difference between
freedom of conscience and freedom of speech. In Canada, nobody can order the accused to cease to believe what he believes.
But we can and do tell him that he has no right to preach what he believes if
his preaching amounts to hatemongering against peoples. On the contrary, the
people of Canada have decided
it is a crime for him to preach like that. And he is not above the law.

[
19
]

We turn finally to the crucial mitigating factor
relied upon by the trial judge. While we think it inappropriate to describe the
accused as “ground down” by the charges against him, we think it appropriate to
consider the other consequences visited upon him for his crime.

[
20
]

We do not consider mere delay in sentencing to
be a mitigating factor in a case where the delay is not the fault of the Crown.

A.B.C.
(1992)
1991 ABCA 337 (CanLII)
, 120 A.R. 106. (Alta C.A.). Nor is pre-charge delay a
significant factor in a disposition where the paramount sentencing factors are,
like here, general deterrence and denunciation.
Spence
(1993)
1992 ABCA 352 (CanLII)
, 78 C.C.C.
(3d) 451. But a long history between the commencement and the end of a criminal
prosecution, and a long record of unusual litigation steps, even if not the
fault of the Crown, can be viewed as a mitigating factor for sentence because
of the added expense for the accused and the extended anxiety for him and his
family.
Cooper No. 2
(1977)
1977 CanLII 2103 (ON CA)
, 35 C.C.C. 35 (Ont. C.A.),
Zundel No 2

(unreported Ontario May 13,
1988).

[
21
]

In this regard, the record here is quite
remarkable and, fortunately, unique. The indictment in this case was preferred
on June 26, 1984. The matter has come before the courts for nine major events
during the succeeding 12 years. The prolix history of this case is almost
without precedent and, it should be said, is the fault of nobody. First, the
accused brought a motion to quash on the grounds that the charging section was
unconstitutional, which was dismissed in 1985 in Queen’s Bench.
Keegstra

(1985),
1984 CanLII 1313 (AB QB)
, 19 C.C.C. (3d) 254. Then he went to trial. He was convicted by a jury,
and condemned to pay a fine of $5,000. He appealed his conviction, and this
Court on June 6, 1988, decided that the charging section offended the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. Keeastra
(1988)
1988 ABCA 234 (CanLII)
, 43 C.C.C. (3d) 150. The
Crown appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, and it reversed our decision on
the
Charter
question, and returned the matter to us for decision on the
other grounds of appeal raised by the accused, which included an argument that
he had been unfairly deprived of a reasonable opportunity to pursue a challenge
of the jurors for cause.
Keeastra

1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 697. We allowed that
ground of appeal and ordered a new trial.
Keeastra

1991 ABCA 97 (CanLII)
, [1991] 4 W.W.R. 136.
In 1992, he again went to trial before a jury and was again convicted. He again
appealed to this Court, and was again successful in obtaining an order for a
new trial before a divided panel on the question whether a jury question has
received an adequate reply.
Keegstra
(1994)
1994 ABCA 293 (CanLII)
, 92 C.C.C. (3d) 505. The
Crown again appealed to the Supreme Court, again with success, and the
conviction was restored.
Keegstra

1996 CanLII 221 (SCC)
, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 458. The Crown now
proceeds with its appeal on sentence, which had been left pending these past
four years.

[
22
]

In the light of these very special
circumstances, and for no other reason we would suspend the sentence of one
year in prison we would otherwise have imposed, and release the accused on
probation for that period. This should not be taken as any sort of vindication.
Indeed, to emphasize this, and his lack of remorse for his criminal acts, we
would impose 200 hours community service, preferably in service of those who
have come to Canada as victims
of racial, religious, or ethnic hatred elsewhere. We direct that the probation
service make a report to this panel every three months on the performance of
this term. The order need not contain any other special terms, but will contain
the term that he keep the peace. This includes of course that he must not
attempt to preach hatred of the Jewish people to anybody, including
hatemongering that is thinly disguised as historical research. To avoid
misunderstanding, this will be an explicit term of the order.

JUDGMENT DATED
at CALGARY, Alberta,

this 26th day of September,

A.D. 1996
